claim: Peptidase-containing ATP-binding cassette transporters (PCATs) are unique members of the ABC transporter family that proteolytically process and export peptides and proteins.
source: The peptidase-containing ATP-binding cassette transporters (PCATs) are unique members of the ABC transporter family that proteolytically process and export peptides and proteins.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about PCATs presented in the abstract, supported by the broader scientific literature on ABC transporters.

claim: Each PCAT contains two peptidase domains that cleave off the secretion signal.
source: Each PCAT contains two peptidase domains that cleave off the secretion signal, two transmembrane domains forming a translocation pathway, and two nucleotide-binding domains that hydrolyze ATP.
evidence: This structural description is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript and prior knowledge of PCAT architecture.

claim: Each PCAT contains two transmembrane domains forming a translocation pathway.
source: Each PCAT contains two peptidase domains that cleave off the secretion signal, two transmembrane domains forming a translocation pathway, and two nucleotide-binding domains that hydrolyze ATP.
evidence: This structural description is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript and prior knowledge of PCAT architecture.

claim: Each PCAT contains two nucleotide-binding domains that hydrolyze ATP.
source: Each PCAT contains two peptidase domains that cleave off the secretion signal, two transmembrane domains forming a translocation pathway, and two nucleotide-binding domains that hydrolyze ATP.
evidence: This structural description is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript and prior knowledge of PCAT architecture.

claim: Crystal structures of PCAT1 from Clostridium thermocellum were previously determined in the absence and presence of ATP.
source: Previously the crystal structures of a PCAT from Clostridium thermocellum (PCAT1) were determined in the absence and presence of ATP, revealing how ATP binding regulates the protease activity and access to the translocation pathway.
evidence: This refers to prior published work on PCAT1 structures.

claim: ATP binding regulates the protease activity and access to the translocation pathway in PCAT1.
source: Previously the crystal structures of a PCAT from Clostridium thermocellum (PCAT1) were determined in the absence and presence of ATP, revealing how ATP binding regulates the protease activity and access to the translocation pathway.
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies of PCAT1.

claim: The structure of the PCAT1-CtA complex was determined by electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) to 3.4 Å resolution.
source: To address this question, we determined the structure of the PCAT1-CtA complex by electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) to 3.4 Å resolution.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data and methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Two CtAs are bound to PCAT1 via their N-terminal leader peptides.
source: The structure shows that two CtAs are bound via their N-terminal leader peptides, but only one is positioned for cleavage and translocation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only one of the two bound CtAs is positioned for cleavage and translocation.
source: The structure shows that two CtAs are bound via their N-terminal leader peptides, but only one is positioned for cleavage and translocation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure and supported by structural analysis.

claim: ABC transporters use the chemical energy of ATP to transport substrates across biological membranes.
source: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters are ubiquitous membrane proteins that use the chemical energy of ATP to transport substrates across biological membranes (Locher, 2016; Srikant and Gaudet, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Substrates of ABC transporters range from small ions to large lipids and proteins.
source: Substrates of ABC transporters range from small ions to large lipids and proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC transporter substrate diversity.

claim: In gram-positive bacteria, PCATs function both as maturation proteases and exporters to secrete quorum-sensing or antimicrobial polypeptides.
source: In gram-positive bacteria, PCATs function both as maturation proteases and exporters to secrete quorum-sensing or antimicrobial polypeptides (Fath and Kolter, 1993; Håvarstein et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on PCAT function in gram-positive bacteria.

claim: In gram-negative bacteria, PCATs interact with two other membrane proteins to form the Type I secretion system (T1SS).
source: In gram-negative bacteria, PCATs interact with two other membrane proteins to form the Type I secretion system (T1SS), a continuous channel penetrating both the inner and outer membranes (Binet et al., 1997; Michiels et al., 2001; Thomas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on T1SS structure and function.

claim: The Type I secretion system forms a continuous channel penetrating both the inner and outer membranes.
source: In gram-negative bacteria, PCATs interact with two other membrane proteins to form the Type I secretion system (T1SS), a continuous channel penetrating both the inner and outer membranes (Binet et al., 1997; Michiels et al., 2001; Thomas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on T1SS structure.

claim: PCATs were first described 20 years ago.
source: Although PCATs were first described 20 years ago and are essential to prokaryotic life (Håvarstein et al., 1995), structural and functional studies of these proteins have been limited.
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citation.

claim: PCATs are essential to prokaryotic life.
source: Although PCATs were first described 20 years ago and are essential to prokaryotic life (Håvarstein et al., 1995), structural and functional studies of these proteins have been limited.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: PCATs are typically homodimers.
source: PCATs are typically homodimers; each subunit consists of a transmembrane domain (TMD), a nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) characteristic of all ABC transporters, and a unique C39 cysteine peptidase (PEP) domain essential in recruiting the substrate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCAT structure.

claim: Each PCAT subunit consists of a transmembrane domain (TMD), a nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), and a C39 cysteine peptidase (PEP) domain.
source: PCATs are typically homodimers; each subunit consists of a transmembrane domain (TMD), a nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) characteristic of all ABC transporters, and a unique C39 cysteine peptidase (PEP) domain essential in recruiting the substrate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCAT domain architecture.

claim: The C39 cysteine peptidase (PEP) domain is essential in recruiting the substrate.
source: PCATs are typically homodimers; each subunit consists of a transmembrane domain (TMD), a nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) characteristic of all ABC transporters, and a unique C39 cysteine peptidase (PEP) domain essential in recruiting the substrate.
evidence: This is supported by the structural and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In Gram-positive bacteria, substrates of PCATs are synthesized as precursors with an N-terminal leader peptide and a C-terminal cargo peptide.
source: In Gram-positive bacteria, substrates of PCATs are synthesized as precursors with an N-terminal leader peptide and a C-terminal cargo peptide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCAT substrate structure in gram-positive bacteria.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of the leader peptide at the conserved double-glycine motif is necessary for cargo secretion.
source: Proteolytic cleavage of the leader peptide at the conserved double-glycine motif is necessary for cargo secretion (Nishie et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The substrates of the T1SS in Gram-negative bacteria are typically large proteins containing a C-terminal secretion signal that is not subjected to proteolytic processing.
source: The substrates of the T1SS in Gram-negative bacteria are typically large proteins containing a C-terminal secretion signal that is not subjected to proteolytic processing (Lecher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Crystal structures of isolated peptidase domains and NBDs have been reported for several PCATs.
source: Crystal structures of isolated peptidase domains and NBDs have been reported for several PCATs (Lecher et al., 2012; Ishii et al., 2010; Ishii et al., 2013; Schmitt et al., 2003; Bobeica et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior structural work.

claim: The structures of a full-length transporter, PCAT1 from Clostridium thermocellum, were determined by X-ray crystallography.
source: Recently, the structures of a full-length transporter, PCAT1 from Clostridium thermocellum, were determined by X-ray crystallography (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The structure of PCAT1 in the absence of ATP and substrate reveals a large α-helical barrel sufficient to accommodate a small protein.
source: The structure of PCAT1 in the absence of ATP and substrate reveals a large α-helical barrel sufficient to accommodate a small protein.
evidence: This is based on prior structural work on PCAT1.

claim: In the inward-facing conformation, the protein-secretion pathway of PCAT1 is open to the cytosol and closed to the extracellular side.
source: Typical of an inward-facing ATP transporter, the protein-secretion pathway is open to the cytosol and closed to the extracellular side.
evidence: This is based on prior structural work on PCAT1 and general knowledge of ABC transporter conformations.

claim: In the apo state, the NBDs of PCAT1 are semi-separated.
source: The NBDs are semi-separated and the PEP domains dock onto the intracellular openings of the translocation pathway.
evidence: This is based on prior structural work on PCAT1.

claim: In the apo state, the PEP domains dock onto the intracellular openings of the translocation pathway.
source: The NBDs are semi-separated and the PEP domains dock onto the intracellular openings of the translocation pathway.
evidence: This is based on prior structural work on PCAT1.

claim: The structure of ATP-bound PCAT1 shows a closed NBD dimer and an occluded translocation pathway.
source: The structure of an ATP-bound PCAT1 shows a closed NBD dimer and an occluded translocation pathway.
evidence: This is based on prior structural work on PCAT1.

claim: The two PEP domains are not resolved in the ATP-bound structure of PCAT1.
source: The two PEP domains are not resolved in the structure, suggesting that they are flexibly attached to the transporter core.
evidence: This is based on prior structural work on PCAT1.

claim: The PEP domains are flexibly attached to the transporter core in the ATP-bound state.
source: The two PEP domains are not resolved in the structure, suggesting that they are flexibly attached to the transporter core.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of density in the ATP-bound structure.

claim: A key feature that renders CFTR an ion channel instead of a transporter is the 'broken' intracellular gate.
source: A key feature that renders CFTR an ion channel instead of a transporter is the 'broken' intracellular gate: in the NBD-dimerized conformation, an opening in the TM helical bundle connects the ion-conduction pathway to the cytosol (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on CFTR structure.

claim: In CFTR's NBD-dimerized conformation, an opening in the TM helical bundle connects the ion-conduction pathway to the cytosol.
source: A key feature that renders CFTR an ion channel instead of a transporter is the 'broken' intracellular gate: in the NBD-dimerized conformation, an opening in the TM helical bundle connects the ion-conduction pathway to the cytosol (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on CFTR structure.

claim: The 'broken' intracellular gate feature is not observed in PCAT1.
source: This feature is not observed in PCAT1.
evidence: This is based on comparison of PCAT1 structure with CFTR.

claim: The intracellular gate of PCAT1 is closed off upon NBD-dimerization.
source: Like other ATP-driven pumps (Dawson and Locher, 2006; Kim and Chen, 2018; Johnson and Chen, 2018; Hofmann et al., 2019), the intracellular gate of PCAT1 is closed off upon NBD-dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by structural data and comparison with other ABC transporters.

claim: PCAT1 functions through the classic alternating-access mechanism.
source: Thus, we suggest that PCAT1 functions through the classic alternating-access mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparisons with other ABC transporters.

claim: CtA is a small protein consisting of a 24-residue leader peptide followed by a 66-residue cargo peptide.
source: The PCAT1 substrate, CtA, is a small protein consisting of a 24-residue leader peptide followed by a 66-residue cargo peptide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CtA substrate structure.

claim: The protease activity of PCAT1 is specific and is inhibited by ATP-binding.
source: The protease activity of PCAT1 is specific and is inhibited by ATP-binding (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited prior work.

claim: The presence of substrate does not stimulate ATP hydrolysis of PCAT1.
source: Different from most ABC transporters, the presence of substrate does not stimulate ATP hydrolysis of PCAT1 (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited prior work.

claim: The PCAT1 homodimer remains intact during native MS analysis in UDM and C8E4.
source: First, we tested if the PCAT1 homodimer remains intact during native MS analysis in two different detergents: n-undecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside (UDM) and octyl tetraethylene glycol ether (C8E4).
evidence: This is supported by the native MS data presented in the manuscript.

claim: C8E4 requires the lowest activation energy for detergent removal in the gas phase with minimal destabilization of membrane protein complexes during MS analysis.
source: C8E4 has been shown to require the lowest activation energy for detergent removal in the gas phase with minimal destabilization of membrane protein complexes during MS analysis (Reading et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The mass spectra obtained in both UDM and C8E4 yielded a single peak series with a measured mass consistent with the mass of dimeric PCAT1.
source: The mass spectra obtained in both detergents at optimal MS parameters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) yielded a single peak series with a measured mass consistent with the mass of dimeric PCAT1 (Figure 1A and Table 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the native MS data shown in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: Two main assemblies of 172.3 and 182.5 kDa were observed for PCAT1(C21A) with CtA, corresponding to dimeric PCAT1 bound to one or two CtA, respectively.
source: In both detergents, we observed two main assemblies of 172.3 and 182.5 kDa, corresponding to dimeric PCAT1 bound to one or two CtA, respectively (Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the native MS data shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: The PCAT1 dimer with two CtA bound (1:2 complex) is the dominant assembly in the presence of excess CtA.
source: Based on the relative peak intensities with correction for gas-phase dissociation, the PCAT1 dimer with two CtA bound (1:2 complex) is the dominant assembly in the presence of excess CtA (75 ± 2% in UDM and 84 ± 2% in C8E4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Table 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the native MS data with quantitative analysis.

claim: The lower abundance of the 1:2 complex in UDM is likely due to the higher collision activation energies needed to remove UDM that lead to increased protein complex dissociation.
source: The lower abundance of the 1:2 complex in UDM is likely due to the higher collision activation energies needed to remove UDM that lead to increased protein complex dissociation (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the MS data showing different activation energies required for different detergents.

claim: The overall resolution of the PCAT1(C21A)-CtA complex cryo-EM structure is approximately 3.4 Å.
source: The overall resolution is approximately 3.4 Å (Figure 2, Table 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM data and resolution estimation.

claim: Side-chain densities are prominent in the TMDs, allowing unambiguous residue assignment.
source: Side-chain densities are prominent in the TMDs, allowing unambiguous residue assignment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: The density of the PEPs and NBDs show clear definition of secondary structure.
source: The density of the PEPs and NBDs show clear definition of secondary structure, permitting docking of the crystal structures of isolated PEP and NBD.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: Extra densities unaccounted by PCAT1 are found on the surface of both PEP domains, likely corresponding to the N-terminal region of CtA.
source: Extra densities, unaccounted by PCAT1, are found on the surface of both PEP domains, likely corresponding to the N-terminal region of CtA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps and interpreted based on the known structure.

claim: The final model contains residues 8–722 of PCAT1 and two leader peptides of CtA.
source: The final model, containing residues 8–722 of PCAT1 and two leader peptides of CtA, was refined against the EM density to excellent geometry and statistics (Table 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the description of the final structural model.

claim: In the ATP-free, substrate-bound conformation, the TM cavity is continuous with the cytosol and closed off to the extracellular space.
source: In this ATP-free, substrate-bound conformation, the TM cavity is continuous with the cytosol and closed off to the extracellular space.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The two PEP domains, each binding a CtA molecule, interact with the transporter core at the TMD/NBD interface.
source: The two PEP domains, each binding a CtA molecule, interact with the transporter core at the TMD/NBD interface.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The structure is two-fold symmetric, with the exception of the C-terminal regions of the substrate.
source: The structure is two-fold symmetric, with the exception of the C-terminal regions of the substrate, a point that we will discuss in detail below.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The cleavage site contains a consensus sequence of L(−12)XXXE(−8)L(−7)XXXXG(−2)G(−1).
source: The cleavage site contains a consensus sequence of L(−12)XXXE(−8)L(−7)XXXXG(−2)G(−1) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Residues 8–25 of the leader peptide form a L-shaped structure that wraps around the PEP domain.
source: Residues 8–25 of the leader peptide form a L-shaped structure that wraps around the PEP domain, with the N-terminus in the cytosol and the C-terminal end at the lateral opening of the translocation pathway (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Residues 15–21 of the leader peptide form a short helix, docking onto a hydrophobic groove on PEP.
source: Residues 15–21 (i.e, positions −10 to −4 of the consensus sequence) form a short helix, docking onto a hydrophobic groove on PEP (Figures 3B and 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The double-glycine motif (G23 and G24) is inserted into the active site of PEP.
source: The double-glycine motif (G23 and G24), inserted to the active site of PEP, interacts with catalytic residues C21A and H99 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The total buried surface of the leader peptide by the PEP domain is approximately 740 Å2.
source: The total buried surface of the leader peptide by the PEP domain is approximately 740 Å2.
evidence: This is calculated from the structural data.

claim: The substrate-binding cleft at the cleavage site is very narrow, which explains the specificity for the double-glycine motif in proteolysis.
source: The substrate-binding cleft at the cleavage site is very narrow, which explains the specificity for the double-glycine motif in proteolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the narrow binding cleft.

claim: The Cβ atom of C21 is about 5.5 Å away from G24.
source: The Cβ atom of C21 (mutated to alanine) is about 5.5 Å away from G24, consistent with C21 serving as a nucleophile to attack the substrate backbone (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Schechter and Berger, 1967).
evidence: This is directly measured from the structure.

claim: C21 serves as a nucleophile to attack the substrate backbone.
source: The Cβ atom of C21 (mutated to alanine) is about 5.5 Å away from G24, consistent with C21 serving as a nucleophile to attack the substrate backbone (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Schechter and Berger, 1967).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by cited literature on protease mechanisms.

claim: H99 orients the N atom of its imidazole ring towards C21A.
source: H99 orients the N atom of its imidazole ring towards the C21A, consistent with its role to polarize the attacking C21 (Husain and Lowe, 1968; Wu and Tai, 2004).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and supported by cited literature.

claim: H99 functions to polarize the attacking C21.
source: H99 orients the N atom of its imidazole ring towards the C21A, consistent with its role to polarize the attacking C21 (Husain and Lowe, 1968; Wu and Tai, 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by cited literature on protease mechanisms.

claim: The side chain of D115 forms a hydrogen bond with H99.
source: The side chain of D115 forms a hydrogen bond with H99, maintaining H99 in an electronegative state and a catalytically favorable position (Vernet et al., 1995).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and supported by cited literature.

claim: D115 maintains H99 in an electronegative state and a catalytically favorable position.
source: The side chain of D115 forms a hydrogen bond with H99, maintaining H99 in an electronegative state and a catalytically favorable position (Vernet et al., 1995).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by cited literature.

claim: Q15 may function as an oxyanion hole that stabilizes the tetrahedral intermediate.
source: In addition, the highly conserved Q15 residue is located in the vicinity, suggesting that it may function as an oxyanion hole that stabilizes the tetrahedral intermediate (Ménard et al., 1991).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by cited literature on protease mechanisms.

claim: The configuration of the active site is typical of a cysteine protease.
source: The configuration of the active site is typical of a cysteine protease, indicating that PCAT1 processes the CtA substrate via the common catalytic thiol mechanism (Drenth et al., 1968; Kamphuis et al., 1984).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by cited literature on cysteine protease mechanisms.

claim: PCAT1 processes the CtA substrate via the common catalytic thiol mechanism.
source: The configuration of the active site is typical of a cysteine protease, indicating that PCAT1 processes the CtA substrate via the common catalytic thiol mechanism (Drenth et al., 1968; Kamphuis et al., 1984).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by cited literature.

claim: The structure of the PEP domain is highly conserved among different PCATs.
source: The structure of the PEP domain is highly conserved among different PCATs.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons shown in the manuscript.

claim: The overall root-mean-square deviations (RMSDs) among the structures of ComA, LahT147, and the PEP domain of PCAT1 are approximately 1 Å.
source: The overall root-mean-square deviations (RMSDs) among the structures of ComA (Ishii et al., 2010) (PDB: 3K8U), LahT147 (Bobeica et al., 2019) (PDB: 6MPZ), and the PEP domain of PCAT1 are approximately 1 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is calculated from structural comparisons.

claim: Substrates of different PEPs share a consensus leader peptide sequence.
source: In addition, substrates of the different PEPs share a consensus leader peptide sequence (Figure 3A), yet each PEP specifically recognizes one or a small subset of substrates.
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 3A.

claim: Each PEP specifically recognizes one or a small subset of substrates.
source: In addition, substrates of the different PEPs share a consensus leader peptide sequence (Figure 3A), yet each PEP specifically recognizes one or a small subset of substrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PEP substrate specificity.

claim: The leader peptides of CtA and the LahT147 substrate both contain a two-turn helix consisting of residues from positions −10 to −4.
source: The leader peptides of CtA and the LahT147 substrate both contain a two-turn helix consisting of residues from positions −10 to −4, docking into a shallow groove on the surface of the PEP (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison.

claim: A hydrophobic knot is formed by the two leucine residues at positions −7 and −12 of the leader peptide and two hydrophobic residues on PEP.
source: A hydrophobic knot, formed by the two leucine residues at positions −7 and −12 of the leader peptide and two hydrophobic residues on PEP, is observed in both structures (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structures.

claim: The L(−7)A and L(−12)A mutants of CtA have much lower affinity for PCAT1 compared to wild-type CtA.
source: Compared to the wt CtA, the L(−7)A and L(−12)A mutants have much lower affinity for PCAT1.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Hydrophobic residues A55 and I59 on PCAT1 are within the Van der Waals radius of L(−7)A and L(−12)A of CtA.
source: We found hydrophobic residues A55 and I59 on PCAT1 that are within the Van der Waals radius of L(−7)A and L(−12)A, and are conserved in LahT147 as well (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: Mutations of residues A55 and I59 of PCAT1 lowered its affinity for CtA by more than eight fold.
source: Furthermore, reciprocal mutations introduced to residues A55 and I59 of PCAT1 lowered its affinity for CtA (Figure 4E) by more than eight fold, consistent with the role that these residues play on the CtA recognition.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The hydrophobic interaction involving L(−7) and L(−12) is likely a common feature shared by different PEP domains.
source: This hydrophobic interaction is likely a common feature shared by different PEP domains.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparisons and mutational data.

claim: Alanine substitution of either one of the two leucine residues in the ComA substrate decreased its affinity by approximately twenty fold.
source: Alanine substitution of either one of the two leucine residues in the ComA substrate decreased its affinity by approximately twenty fold (Kotake et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: LahT147 does not process precursor peptides with substitutions at L(−7) or L(−12).
source: Similarly, LahT147 does not process precursor peptides with substitutions at L(−7) or L(−12) (Bobeica et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The residue at position −4 is important for the PEP-substrate interaction.
source: Mutational data at the −4 position indicate that this residue is also important for the PEP-substrate interaction (Figure 4D and Kotake et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by mutational data and cited literature.

claim: The amino acid identity at position −4 varies among different substrates.
source: however, in contrast to the highly conserved L(−7) and L(−12) residues, the amino acid identity at position −4 varies among different substrates (Figure 3A and C) and appears to correlate with the interacting residue on PEP.
evidence: This is observed from sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: M(−4) of CtA packs against G135 of PCAT1.
source: For example, M (−4) of CtA packs against G135 of PCAT1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: V(−4) of the LahT147 substrate interacts with I137 on PEP.
source: In LahT147, a much smaller residue V(−4) of the substrate interacts with a larger residue I137 on PEP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: The leader peptide position −4 confers specificity among different PCATs.
source: Therefore, it seems that the leader peptide position −4 confers specificity among different PCATs.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and mutational data.

claim: The cargo region (residues 25–90) of CtA is flexible and less defined.
source: In contrast to the leader peptide, the cargo region (residues 25–90) is flexible and less defined.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: Density of elongated shape is observed inside the translocation pathway, packed along the interior surface of the cavity.
source: Inside the translocation pathway, we observe density of elongated shape packed along the interior surface of the cavity shown in the composite cryo-EM map of PCAT1 and CtA (Figure 5A, colored blue).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: Cysteines at multiple positions along CtA can be crosslinked to K275C and A433C on PCAT1.
source: Cysteines at multiple positions along CtA can be crosslinked to K275C and A433C on PCAT1, suggesting that the cargo inside the cavity is unstructured and flexible, consistent with the amorphous nature of the EM density (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The cargo inside the cavity is unstructured and flexible.
source: Cysteines at multiple positions along CtA can be crosslinked to K275C and A433C on PCAT1, suggesting that the cargo inside the cavity is unstructured and flexible, consistent with the amorphous nature of the EM density (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is inferred from the crosslinking data and EM density.

claim: The cysteine at position 38 of CtA can be weakly crosslinked to K275C but not to K433C.
source: The cysteine at position 38 of CtA can be weakly crosslinked to K275C but not to K433C, which is consistent with the structure.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the crosslinking experiments.

claim: K38 of CtA is near the leader peptide at the cytoplasmic side of the membrane and is not able to reach the extracellular ceiling of the cavity prior to proteolytic cleavage.
source: K38 is near the leader peptide at the cytoplasmic side of the membrane and is not able to reach the extracellular ceiling of the cavity prior to proteolytic cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the structure and crosslinking data.

claim: No crosslinking product was observed for the cysteine placed outside the TM cavity (K417C).
source: No crosslinking product was observed for the cysteine placed outside the TM cavity (K417C), indicating that the reaction is specific (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the crosslinking experiments.

claim: The density inside the TM cavity appears to be connected to only one of the two leader peptides.
source: The density inside the TM cavity appears to be connected to only one of the two leader peptides (Figure 5A and D), raising the question whether one or two cargos are inside the TM cavity.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: The volume of the TM cavity is estimated to be 15,000 Å3.
source: Using the 3V server (Voss and Gerstein, 2010), the volume of the TM cavity is estimated to be 15,000 Å3.
evidence: This is calculated using computational tools.

claim: The size of a CtA cargo is approximately 9000 Å3.
source: Considering the average density of a small protein is around 1.35 g/cm (Voss and Gerstein, 2010; Fischer et al., 2009), the size of a CtA cargo is approximately 9000 Å3, a conservative estimate for an unstructured protein.
evidence: This is calculated based on known protein densities and the molecular weight of CtA cargo.

claim: It is likely that only one cargo is inserted into the TM cavity.
source: Thus, it is likely that only one cargo is inserted into the TM cavity.
evidence: This is inferred from volume calculations and structural observations.

claim: The translocating substrate inserts its C-terminal cargo into the TM cavity.
source: We termed the cargo inside the TM cavity the 'translocating CtA' as it is positioned for cleavage and translocation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The substrate specificity is conferred through the leader peptide only.
source: The density for the cargo region is weak and amorphous, suggesting that there is no specific interaction between the cargo and transporter, and the substrate specificity is conferred through the leader peptide only.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of specific cargo-transporter interactions in the structure.

claim: For the non-translocating CtA, no density is observed beyond S26.
source: For the other substrate, the non-translocating CtA, no density is observed beyond S26, two residues beyond the double glycine motif (Figure 5D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: G23, G24, and S25 of the non-translocating CtA form a kink, orienting the C-terminus towards the cytoplasm.
source: Furthermore, G23, G24, and S25 form a kink, orienting the C-terminus towards the cytoplasm (Figure 5D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The PCAT1-CtA complex can be pulled down using an antibody against a tag placed at the C-terminus of CtA.
source: There is also biochemical evidence that the C-terminus of CtA is accessible: the PCAT1-CtA complex can be pulled down using an antibody against a tag placed at the C-terminus of CtA (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited prior work.

claim: The non-translocating cargo is located in the cytosol, flexibly linked to the leader peptide.
source: Based on these observations, we suggest that the non-translocating cargo is located in the cytosol, flexibly linked to the leader peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and biochemical data.

claim: In the substrate-bound conformation, the intracellular opening of the TM cavity is approximately 3 Å wider than in the apo state.
source: Comparing the structures of PCAT1 in the presence and absence of CtA shows that in the substrate-bound conformation, the intracellular opening of the TM cavity (formed from TM3 and TM4) is approximately 3 Å wider and the two NBDs are further apart (Figure 6).
evidence: This is directly measured from structural comparison.

claim: The two NBDs are further apart in the substrate-bound conformation compared to the apo state.
source: Comparing the structures of PCAT1 in the presence and absence of CtA shows that in the substrate-bound conformation, the intracellular opening of the TM cavity (formed from TM3 and TM4) is approximately 3 Å wider and the two NBDs are further apart (Figure 6).
evidence: This is directly measured from structural comparison.

claim: The structural differences between apo and substrate-bound PCAT1 are not influenced by crystal packing.
source: These structural differences are not influenced by crystal packing, as regions involved in lattice contacts do not undergo conformational changes upon CtA binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of crystal contacts.

claim: The conformational change of PCAT1 upon substrate binding is opposite to that of the multidrug transporter MRP1.
source: The conformational change of PCAT1 is opposite to that of the multidrug transporter MRP1, in which substrate binding brings the two NBDs closer (Johnson and Chen, 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited literature on MRP1.

claim: In MRP1, substrate binding brings the two NBDs closer.
source: The conformational change of PCAT1 is opposite to that of the multidrug transporter MRP1, in which substrate binding brings the two NBDs closer (Johnson and Chen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: MRP1 has higher ATPase activity in the presence of its substrate.
source: MRP1, like many other ABC transporters, has higher ATPase activity in the presence of its substrate (Johnson and Chen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Addition of CtA reduces the ATPase activity of wild-type PCAT1 by about 10%.
source: In contrast, addition of CtA reduces the ATPase activity of PCAT1 by about 10% for the wild-type protein and 50% for the cleavage-incompetent C21A mutant (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited prior work.

claim: Addition of CtA reduces the ATPase activity of PCAT1(C21A) by 50%.
source: In contrast, addition of CtA reduces the ATPase activity of PCAT1 by about 10% for the wild-type protein and 50% for the cleavage-incompetent C21A mutant (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited prior work.

claim: ATP hydrolysis requires NBD dimerization.
source: As ATP hydrolysis requires NBD dimerization, the structural observation correlates well with the distinct biochemical property of this protein-conducting ABC transporter.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC transporter mechanism.

claim: The insertion of a large cargo into the TM cavity would likely decrease the rate of NBD dimerization thereby slowing down ATP hydrolysis.
source: The insertion of a large cargo into the TM cavity would likely decrease the rate of NBD dimerization thereby slowing down ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and biochemical data.

claim: Binding of the leader peptide induces local conformational changes within the PEP domain.
source: Binding of the leader peptide also induces local conformational changes within the PEP domain.
evidence: This is directly observed by structural comparison.

claim: The largest displacement upon leader peptide binding occurs in a loop (residues 91–98) preceding the catalytic residue H99, approximately 5 Å.
source: The largest displacement, approximately 5 Å, occurs in a loop (residues 91–98) preceding the catalytic residue H99 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is directly measured from structural comparison.

claim: In the substrate-bound structure, a path between the catalytic site and the TM cavity opens up permitting insertion of the C-terminal cargo into the translocation pathway.
source: As a result, in the substrate-bound structure, a path between the catalytic site and the TM cavity opens up permitting insertion of the C-terminal cargo into the translocation pathway at the lateral opening between TM3 and TM4. (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: ABC importers largely depend on binding proteins to confer substrate selectivity.
source: The current understanding is that ABC importers largely depend on binding proteins to confer substrate selectivity while exporters interact with their substrate directly through their TMDs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the ABC transporter field.

claim: ABC exporters interact with their substrate directly through their TMDs.
source: The current understanding is that ABC importers largely depend on binding proteins to confer substrate selectivity while exporters interact with their substrate directly through their TMDs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the ABC transporter field.

claim: Structures of ABC exporters reveal a well-defined, substrate-binding site at the interface of the two TMDs.
source: The structures of ABC exporters, such as the multidrug transporters MRP1 (Johnson and Chen, 2017), ABCG2 (Manolaridis et al., 2018), P-glycoprotein (Alam et al., 2019), the Lipid A flipase MsbA (Mi et al., 2017), LPS transporter LptB2FG (Li et al., 2019), and the promiscuous exporter TmrAB (Hofmann et al., 2019), all reveal a well-defined, substrate-binding site at the interface of the two TMDs.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies of ABC exporters.

claim: Polypeptides are recognized by PCATs through a different mechanism than typical ABC exporters.
source: Here we present a different mechanism by which polypeptides are recognized by PCATs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the structural data presented.

claim: The cytosolic peptidase domain binds substrate through its N-terminal secretion sequence.
source: Instead of the TMDs, the cytosolic peptidase domain binds substrate through its N-terminal secretion sequence, that is the leader peptide.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The common feature shared by PCATs is a hydrophobic knot formed by two residues of the peptidase domain and residues at positions −7 and −12 of the leader peptide.
source: The common feature shared by PCATs is a hydrophobic knot formed by two residues of the peptidase domain and residues at positions −7 and −12 of the leader peptide.
evidence: This is observed in the structures and supported by mutational data.

claim: The TMDs of PCAT1 do not provide any specific binding region for the cargo.
source: Unlike most ABC exporters, the TMDs of PCAT1 do not provide any specific binding region for the cargo.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The TMDs of PCAT1 merely provide a large conduit to transverse the lipid bilayer.
source: Instead, they merely provide a large conduit to transverse the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The PCAT system can be used to secrete different cargo proteins that are tethered to the same secretion signal.
source: This observation explains why the PCAT system can be used to secrete different cargo proteins that are tethered to the same secretion signal (van Belkum et al., 1997).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and supported by cited literature.

claim: The absence of a high-affinity binding site in the TMDs is reminiscent of the E. coli cobalamin importer BtuCD.
source: The absence of a high-affinity binding site in the TMDs is reminiscent of the E. coli cobalamin importer BtuCD, where the substrate is recruited by the periplasmic binding protein and the TMDs provide a teflon-like pathway for conduction (Korkhov et al., 2012; Korkhov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature on BtuCD.

claim: PCAT1 adopts an inward-facing conformation in the absence of ATP.
source: PCAT1 adopts an inward-facing conformation in the absence of ATP, in which the NBD interface is open and each PEP domain docks onto a lateral opening of the TM pathway.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and supported by prior structural work.

claim: Two substrates can bind to PCAT simultaneously.
source: Two substrates can bind to PCAT simultaneously, but only one substrate is positioned for cleavage and translocation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and supported by native MS data.

claim: The translocating substrate inserts its C-terminal cargo into the TM cavity and the corresponding PEP domain cleaves the substrate to free the cargo.
source: The translocating substrate inserts its C-terminal cargo into the TM cavity and the corresponding PEP domain cleaves the substrate to free the cargo.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on structural observations.

claim: ATP binding brings the two NBDs into close contact, orienting the translocation pathway towards the extracellular space.
source: ATP binding brings the two NBDs into close contact, orienting the translocation pathway towards the extracellular space.
evidence: This is based on prior structural work on ATP-bound PCAT1 and general knowledge of ABC transporter mechanism.

claim: The TM pathway confers no specific binding of the substrate.
source: As the TM pathway confers no specific binding of the substrate, the cargo will be released and, subsequently, the TMDs will isomerize to form the occluded conformation where both the extracellular gate and the cytoplasmic gate are closed (PDB: 4S0F).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: Formation of the closed NBD dimer disengages the PEP domains from the core transporter permitting release of the leader peptide and binding of a new substrate.
source: Formation of the closed NBD dimer disengages the PEP domains from the core transporter permitting release of the leader peptide and binding of a new substrate.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on structural observations and prior work.

claim: ATP hydrolysis and ADP release reset the transporter to the inward-facing conformation allowing the PEP to dock back and position one of the two substrates for cleavage and translocation.
source: ATP hydrolysis and ADP release reset the transporter to the inward-facing conformation allowing the PEP to dock back and position one of the two substrates for cleavage and translocation.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on structural observations and knowledge of ABC transporter cycles.

claim: A key aspect of the transport model is the strict coupling of substrate cleavage to translocation.
source: A key aspect of this model is the strict coupling of substrate cleavage to translocation.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on structural observations.

claim: In the inward-facing conformation where two substrates are bound, the non-translocating substrate adopts a kink at the double-glycine motif, preventing uncoupled cleavage.
source: In the inward-facing conformation where two substrates are bound, the non-translocating substrate adopts a kink at the double-glycine motif, preventing uncoupled cleavage.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: In the ATP-bound conformation, the disengaged PEP domains have little proteolytic activity.
source: In the ATP-bound conformation, the disengaged PEP domains have little proteolytic activity as the transporter core is necessary for substrate cleavage (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited prior work.

claim: The transporter core is necessary for substrate cleavage.
source: In the ATP-bound conformation, the disengaged PEP domains have little proteolytic activity as the transporter core is necessary for substrate cleavage (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited prior work.

claim: Strict coupling of cleavage to translocation is important to prevent the uncontrolled release of cargo molecules into the cytosol of the secreting cells.
source: This strict coupling is important to prevent the uncontrolled release of cargo molecules, some of which are toxic, into the cytosol of the secreting cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and biological function.
